title: External Trade
summary: External trade (foreign or international trade) is buying and selling of goods and services across national boundaries; it arises from uneven distribution of natural resources and specialisation. In India, trade policy is framed by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Types: import trade (purchase of goods from a firm of another country), export trade (sale of goods to a firm of another country) and entrepot trade (re-export: importing goods in order to export them, with or without change, e.g. an Indian firm imports rubber from Thailand and exports it to Japan). Reasons for entrepot trade: non-accessible trade routes, processing or finishing required, and lack of trade agreement between the two countries. Visible trade is import and export of tangible goods (merchandise trade); invisible trade covers services (shipping, insurance, tourism, technicians, interest).

Importance: promotes specialisation; improves standard of living; enhances competition; generates employment; price equalisation; improves international relations; economic growth; efficient use of natural resources. Difficulties: geographical distance; greater risk (transit, exchange rate); transport and communication; legal and customs restrictions (tariffs, quotas); study of foreign markets; changing rules and regulations; fluctuations in the exchange rate (managed in India by the RBI).

Indent houses help in sending and receiving orders; export houses promote exports (STC, MMTC, HHEC, CCIC); forwarding agents act for exporters in completing shipping formalities; clearing agents act for importers in clearing goods from the port; shipping companies carry goods for freight; insurance companies bear loss or damage to insured goods; trade commissioners are officials appointed by the government in embassies to represent the country's trade interests; trade representatives guide exporters abroad. Requirements: Import Export Code (IEC) number from the Director General of Foreign Trade, and Registration-cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC) from the export promotion council.

(1) Receipt of enquiry and sending quotations; (2) receipt of indent (export order); (3) credit enquiry (letter of credit or bank guarantee); (4) obtaining export licence (with IEC, RCMC and ECGC registration); (5) production or procurement of goods; (6) pre-shipment inspection; (7) excise clearance; (8) packing and marking; (9) appointment of forwarding agent; (10) despatch of goods by rail or road; (11) formalities by the forwarding agent: customs permit, shipping order (agreement with the shipping company to put goods on the ship), shipping bill and payment of export duty (on which customs calculates duty), dock dues (dock challan), customs verification, mate's receipt (issued by the captain after loading), bill of lading (document received in exchange for the mate's receipt; 'freight paid' or 'freight forward'), insurance of cargo and advice to the exporter; (12) export invoice and consular invoice; (13) securing payment through a letter of credit (issued by the importer's bank, ensures payment up to the stated amount) or a letter of hypothecation (authorises the bank to sell the goods if the importer dishonours the bill).

(1) Trade enquiry; (2) obtaining import licence (IEC from DGFT); (3) obtaining foreign exchange from the RBI; (4) placing the indent (purchase order); (5) sending a letter of credit; (6) procuring shipping documents; (7) appointment of clearing agent; (8) formalities by the clearing agent: endorsement of bill of lading for delivery, bill of entry (three copies to customs, which calculates import duty; the importer or clearing agent pays it), payment of dock charges (Port Trust receipt), despatch by rail or road and advice to the importer.

vsa: Mention any two reasons for entrepot trade.
Non-accessibility of trade routes and goods needing processing or finishing (also lack of trade agreement).
How does external trade improve the standard of living of people?
People consume goods they do not produce, and exports earn foreign exchange, raising income and living standards.
How can a clearing agent help the importer?
He completes the customs and dock formalities, pays duty and takes delivery of the goods from the port and sends them to the importer.
A document issued by the importer's bank in favour of the exporter assuring payment of the exporter's bill up to the specified amount.
Visible trade is import and export of goods; invisible trade is exchange of services such as shipping, insurance and tourism.
State any four difficulties faced in external trade.
Geographical distance, greater risk, legal and customs restrictions and exchange rate fluctuations.
sa: Explain the three types of external trade.
Import trade (buying goods from a foreign country), export trade (selling goods to a foreign country) and entrepot trade (importing goods and re-exporting them).
Explain any three roles played by a clearing agent in external trade.
Gets the bill of lading endorsed, files the bill of entry and pays customs duty; pays dock charges and takes delivery; despatches goods to the importer and sends advice.
Explain any three documents used in external trade.
Bill of lading (issued by the shipping company), shipping bill (used by customs to compute export duty) and bill of entry (filed by the importer or clearing agent).
Explain any three importance of external trade.
It promotes specialisation, improves living standards and generates employment.
Explain any three facilitators of external trade.
Indent houses, forwarding agents and insurance companies (also shipping company and trade commissioners).
Explain the difference between a letter of credit and a letter of hypothecation.
A letter of credit is issued by the importer's bank guaranteeing payment; a letter of hypothecation is given by the exporter to his bank authorising it to sell the goods if the bill is dishonoured.
la: Explain the procedure for export trade.
Enquiry and quotation, indent, credit enquiry, export licence, procurement, inspection, excise clearance, packing, forwarding agent and shipping formalities, invoice and securing payment.
Explain the procedure for import trade.
Trade enquiry, import licence, foreign exchange, indent, letter of credit, shipping documents, clearing agent, bill of entry, dock charges, despatch and advice.
Explain the formalities completed by a forwarding agent.
Customs permit, shipping order, shipping bill and export duty, dock dues, customs verification, mate's receipt, bill of lading, insurance and advice to the exporter.
Explain the difficulties faced in external trade.
Distance, risk, transport problems, customs restrictions, market study, changing rules and exchange rate fluctuations.
Explain the importance of external trade.
Specialisation, standard of living, competition, employment, price equalisation, international relations, economic growth and resource utilisation.
